sections.h2: Which office files a Darke County deed?
sections.html:
The Darke County Recorder files it. The office sits in the Greenville courthouse at 504 S. Broadway, answers at 937-547-7390, and posts weekday hours from 8 to 4.

ORC Chapter 317 governs the office, which the county describes as its official keeper of records. Besides deeds and mortgages, the recorder takes mechanic liens, powers of attorney, recognizance bonds, IRS liens, corporate franchise liens and partnership papers. The job is to record what you bring, so a deed written by you or your attorney needs to be finished before it arrives.

sections.h2: What must be done to a deed before the recorder accepts it?
sections.html:
A deed needs the grantor's signature, an acknowledgment, and the auditor's stamp before it goes to the recorder. Under ORC 5301.01, the grantor acknowledges the signing before a judge or clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor, and that official certifies the acknowledgment.

In Darke County the usual order runs like this:

  1. Draft the deed with a legal description that matches the parcel. The county engineer keeps the tax maps and reviews deeds, land transfers and lot splits for proper boundary descriptions.
  2. Sign and acknowledge the deed.
  3. Take the deed and a conveyance fee statement to the Darke County Auditor on the courthouse first floor. The auditor's forms page lists DTE 100 for a standard conveyance, DTE 100EX for an exempt one, DTE 101 for homestead property and DTE 102 for farmland valued at its agricultural use.
  4. Pay the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax to the auditor, get the stamp, and bring the deed to the recorder.

Splitting a lot off a larger parcel adds a step. The county's own contact list sends split questions to the zoning inspector at 937-547-7381, and building permits for the unincorporated areas, the city of Greenville and a list of villages run through the county building regulation office at 937-547-7379.

sections.h2: What are the Darke County recording charges?
sections.html:
The schedule comes from ORC 317.32. A standard deed or mortgage pays a $17 base fee and a $17 housing trust fund fee for its first two pages, then $4 and $4 on every page beyond that. Counties may also charge a preservation surcharge of up to $5 per document, credited to the general fund. Ask the recorder if Darke County collects it and how much.

ServiceFee under ORC 317.32
Record and index, pages 1 and 2$17 base plus $17 housing trust fund
Each added page$4 base plus $4 housing trust fund
Document preservation surchargeUp to $5 per document, at the county's option
Certified copy, per page$1 base plus $1 housing trust fund
Recorder's seal on a certification$0.50 base plus $0.50 housing trust fund
Marginal reference by separate instrument$2 base plus $2 housing trust fund

Source: ORC 317.32 on the Ohio Laws website. The statute makes fees payable when the paper is presented, and it counts each 8.5 by 14 inch page or fraction of one, caption page included.

sections.h2: Which side of a Darke County sale pays the transfer costs?
sections.html:
The seller. Division (D) of ORC 319.202 puts the conveyance fee from section 319.54(G)(3) on the grantor, along with any transfer tax the commissioners have adopted under Chapter 322. That tax is capped at thirty cents per hundred dollars of value, and the grantor pays it to the auditor ahead of recording (ORC 322.02). Ask the Darke County auditor whether a county transfer tax is in place.

The statement of value uses the full consideration, including the amount of any mortgage or vendor's lien. For a gift, it uses the estimated open-market price. Falsifying the value is unlawful. The auditor's website has a calculator that takes the parcel count and sale price and adds the parcel transfer fee, so check the figure there or by phone before closing day.

sections.h2: What does the Darke County auditor check on a deed?
sections.html:
The auditor's stamp tells the recorder the paperwork is complete. Under ORC 319.202, the buyer or the buyer's representative files the value statement, and the auditor indorses the conveyance on its face to show the fee and compliance with the section, keeps the original statement, and sends a copy with the most recent assessed value to the state tax commissioner.

The statement carries two sets of affirmations. One asks whether the seller expects a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction on the current or prior year's tax, and the other asks whether the land was under agricultural valuation. A yes on either calls for a sworn instrument signed by both sides that accounts for the reduction or the recoupment charge. If the property is residential rental property, the auditor's indorsement also reminds the buyer to file the landlord information required by ORC 5323.02.

For a family transfer or other exempt deed, the statement only needs the reason for the exemption. Pick the exempt form (DTE 100EX) and state the reason plainly.

sections.h2: How far back do online Darke County land records reach?
sections.html:
The recorder's page offers an online search of land records beginning May 1996 and says the index was due to reach back to January 1980 by the end of 2023. Ask the office how far back it runs now, and how to view older books in person.

The recorder also offers a free Property Fraud Alert subscription, a notification service meant to warn an owner when a document is recorded against the property. Owners who are about to sell, or who hold a house that has sat vacant, can use it to watch the parcel.

  • Parcel searches, the county map and the sales report live on the auditor's website, not at the recorder.
  • Questions about value or tax on a parcel go to the auditor, and questions about what is already of record go to the recorder.

sections.h2: What history and roads frame Darke County land records?
sections.html:
Settlement began at Fort Jefferson in 1791, and the Treaty of Greenville was signed at Fort Greenville in 1795, ceding southern Ohio to the United States. Darke County was created in 1809 and organized in 1817, the first railroad reached it in 1850, and by the late twentieth century the economy mixed farming with manufacturing while many residents commuted to Dayton.

The 2020 census found 51,881 residents, a median age of 42.5, and 20.8 percent of people at least 65. It counted 20,925 households, 28.8 percent of them one-person households. Land that families have held for decades makes the legal description important, and the county engineer reviews deeds for proper boundary descriptions.

The county's villages include Ansonia, Arcanum, Castine, Gettysburg, Ithaca, New Madison, New Weston, Pitsburg, Union City, Versailles, Wayne Lakes and Yorkshire, and cities, villages and townships hold the zoning authority for their own ground. Main roads include US 127, US 36 and State Routes 49, 47, 121 and 118. A house in an unzoned township answers to the township trustees on zoning, so confirm that before you list.

faqs.q: What is the Darke County Recorder's phone number?
faqs.a: The Darke County Recorder can be reached at 937-547-7390. The office is on the courthouse grounds at 504 S. Broadway in Greenville and keeps weekday hours of 8:00 am to 4:00 pm.

faqs.q: Does the Darke County recorder charge by the page?
faqs.a: Yes. Ohio law sets a charge for the first two pages and a smaller charge for each added page, and the county may add a preservation surcharge of up to $5. The full list is in ORC 317.32.

faqs.q: Do I need the auditor before the recorder in Darke County?
faqs.a: Yes. A deed needs the auditor's conveyance stamp first, which means the conveyance fee statement and fee. After that the recorder files it into the permanent record.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed that I wrote myself?
faqs.a: You can bring one. The deed must be signed and acknowledged before an authorized official, carry a legal description the engineer's tax maps support, and pass the auditor first. Many owners ask a title company or attorney to prepare it.

faqs.q: Are old Darke County deeds searchable online?
faqs.a: Land records are searchable online from May 1996 forward. The recorder's page says the index was due to reach back to January 1980 by the end of 2023, so ask the office how far back it runs now.
